q: P'ei Sung-chih's commentary records a Wei Grand Administrator of a frontier commandery: Sun Ch'üan suddenly arrived with tens of thousands of men, rain had washed out the city palisade and there was no time to repair it, so he ordered everyone in the city to hide while he himself lay in his quarters and did not get up, and Sun Ch'üan withdrew, suspecting an ambush. Who was this man? What difference does P'ei Sung-chih note between this account and the man's main biography?
reply:
## The man

He was **Wen Ping (文聘)**, styled **Zhongye (仲業)**, a man of Wan county in Nanyang, who served Liu Biao and then, after Liu Cong surrendered Jing province, entered Cao Cao's service. Cao Cao made him **Administrator of Jiangxia (江夏太守)**, entrusting him with frontier affairs because Jiangxia bordered Wu:

「太祖先定荊州，江夏與吳接，民心不安，乃以聘為江夏太守，使典北兵，委以邊事，賜爵關內侯。」[20]

## The Pei Songzhi note you're thinking of

The story is in Pei Songzhi's commentary to Wen Ping's biography, quoting the *Wei Lüe* (裴注引《魏略》):

「孫權嘗自將數萬眾卒至。時大雨，城柵崩壞，人民散在田野，未及補治。聘聞權到，不知所施，乃思惟莫若潛默可以疑之。乃敕城中人使不得見，又自臥捨中不起。權果疑之，語其部黨曰：『北方以此人忠臣也，故委之以此郡，今我至而不動，此不有密圖，必當有外救。』遂不敢攻而去。」[1]

That is: Sun Quan came suddenly with tens of thousands; heavy rain had collapsed the city palisade, the people were scattered in the fields, and there was no time to repair it. Wen Ping, not knowing what to do, decided that silent inaction was the best way to make the enemy suspicious. He ordered the townspeople not to show themselves and lay down in his quarters without getting up. Sun Quan indeed grew suspicious and, saying that "the north regards this man as a loyal subject, which is why this commandery was entrusted to him; now I arrive and he does not move — there must be a secret plan or outside relief," did not dare attack and withdrew.

## The difference Pei Songzhi notes

Pei Songzhi's own comment on this note is: 「魏略此語，與本傳反。」[1] — "This statement of the *Wei Lüe* is contrary to the main biography."

The main biography (Chen Shou's text) gives a quite different picture of Sun Quan's attack on Wen Ping at Shiyang:

「孫權以五萬眾自圍聘於石陽，甚急，聘堅守不動，權住二十餘日乃解去。聘追擊破之。增邑五百戶，並前千九百戶。」[19]

So in the *Wei Lüe* version [1], Wen Ping's success was a **ruse of feigned passivity** — he hid his people and stayed in bed, and Sun Quan, suspecting an ambush, left **without attacking**. In the main biography [19], by contrast, Sun Quan **did besiege him** ("甚急"), Wen Ping **held firm without moving** (堅守不動) through a siege lasting more than twenty days, Sun Quan then lifted the siege and left, and Wen Ping **pursued and defeated him** (追擊破之), earning an increase of 500 households. The two accounts therefore disagree both on whether Sun Quan actually attacked and on how the affair ended — which is exactly what Pei Songzhi flags.

(Neither passage records the year of this event, so I will not assign one.)

q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
**The painter was Cao Buxing (曹不興).**

**The record**

The story comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注) to the *Sanguozhi*, in the section on Zhao Da (趙達) of the *Wu shu* biography of Wu Fan, Liu Dun and Zhao Da, where Pei quotes the *Wulu* (《吳錄》). The line reads:

「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏风，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1]

("Cao Buxing was skilled at painting. Quan had him paint a screen; by mistake he let his brush fall and dot the white silk, so he went along with it and made a fly. When it was presented to the throne, Quan took it for a live fly and raised his hand to flick it away.") [1]

So: Cao Buxing was painting a screen at Sun Quan's order; the misplaced brushstroke on the plain silk was turned into a fly, and Sun Quan raised his hand to flick away what he took for a live fly. [1] The "Quan" of the passage is Sun Quan (孫權, 字仲謀).

**Context of the passage**

This line stands at the end of a list of skilled men in Wu given in the same *Wulu* quotation: the calligrapher Huang Xiang (「皇象字休明，廣陵江都人。幼工書」[1]), Yan Wu (「嚴武字子卿，衞尉畯再從子也，圍棊莫與爲輩」[1]), Song Shou (「宋壽占夢，十不失一」[1]) and Zheng Yu (「孤城鄭嫗能相人」[1]), after which the note says 「及範、惇、達八人，世皆稱妙，謂之八絕云」[1] — that with Fan, Dun and Da, eight men were praised in their day and called the "Eight Excellencies" (八絕). The same note goes on to quote the *Jin Yangqiu* (《晉陽秋》), saying 「吳有葛衡字思真，明達天官，能爲機巧，作渾天」[1]. The main text of Zhao Da's section, nearby in the same biography, concerns his calculations and his silence: 「初，孫權行師征伐，每令達有所推步，皆如其言。權問其法，達終不語，由此見薄，祿位不至。」[13]

No further background is needed: the episode in the question agrees with what the *Sanguozhi* commentary records.

q: A wealthy man gave a ride to a woman on the road. She told him she was a messenger from Heaven sent to burn down his house, but because he had been kind to her she let him go home first and move his valuables out. Who was this wealthy man?
reply:
**The wealthy man was Mi Zhu (麋竺), styled Zizhong, of Qu county in Donghai commandery.**

The story is quoted by Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注) to Mi Zhu's biography in the Book of Shu (蜀書), from the 《搜神記》:

「竺嘗從洛歸，未達家數十里，路傍見一婦人，從竺求寄載。行可數里，婦謝去，謂竺曰：「我天使也，當往燒東海麋竺家，感君見載，故以相語。」竺因私請之，婦曰：「不可得不燒。如此，君可馳去，我當緩行，日中火當發。」竺乃還家，遽出財物，日中而火大發。」[1]

(Tr.: Mi Zhu was once returning home from Luo. Some tens of li short of home he saw by the roadside a woman who asked him for a ride. After a few li she thanked him and left, saying: "I am a messenger of Heaven, going to burn down the house of Mi Zhu of Donghai; moved by your giving me a ride, I tell you of it." Mi Zhu privately pleaded with her; she said: "It cannot be that it is not burned. This being so, you may gallop home; I will go slowly, and at midday the fire will break out." Mi Zhu then went home, hurriedly brought out his goods, and at midday a great fire broke out.)

**That he was rich** is stated in the main text of the same biography:

「麋竺字子仲，東海朐人也。祖世貨殖，僮客萬人，貲產鉅億。」[11]

(Tr.: Mi Zhu, styled Zizhong, was a man of Qu in Donghai. For generations his family had been merchants; they had ten thousand servants and retainers, and their property ran into the hundred millions.)

**His link with 先主** is also recorded there:

「竺于是進妹于先主為夫人，奴客二千，金銀貨幣以助軍資，于時困匱，賴此複振。」[11]

(Tr.: Mi Zhu then presented his sister to 先主 as a wife, and two thousand servants and retainers, gold, silver and coin to aid the army's funds; at that time [先主] was in distress and want, and relied on this to revive.) The title of the source block for 先主 reads 先主傳·先主 劉備 [10], i.e. 先主 here is Liu Bei.

Note that this fire story comes from the 《搜神記》 as quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary; the main text of Mi Zhu's biography does not contain it.

After a few li she thanked him and left, saying: "I am a messenger of Heaven, going to burn down the house of Mi Zhu of Donghai; moved by your giving me a ride, I tell you of it." Mi Zhu privately pleaded with her; she said: "It cannot be that it is not burned. This being so, you may gallop home; I will go slowly, and at midday the fire will break out." Mi Zhu then went home, hurriedly brought out his goods, and at midday a great fire broke out.)

(Tr.: Mi Zhu then presented his sister to 先主 as a wife, and two thousand servants and retainers, gold, silver and coin to aid the army's funds; at that time [先主] was in distress and want, and relied on this to revive.) q: A woman from Jiuquan avenged her father by stabbing his killer to death in broad daylight in front of the city post-house, then went to the county office and gave herself up. Who was she, and in which year did this happen?
reply:
## 结论

她是 **龐娥親 (Pang E-qin)** —— 酒泉郡祿福縣人趙君安的女儿、表氏縣龐子夏的妻子，也是龐淯的母亲。她为父报仇、在都亭前白日刺杀李寿一事，按裴注所引皇甫谧《列女传》的记载，发生在 **光和二年 (179年)** 二月上旬。

## 依据

**一、她是谁（姓名、身份）**

陈寿正文称她为龐淯之母"娥"：

> 「初，淯外祖父趙安為同縣李壽所殺，淯舅兄弟三人同時病死，壽家喜。淯母娥自傷父讎不報，乃幃車袖劍，白日刺壽於都亭前」[13]

裴注引皇甫谧《列女传》给出了完整的身份：

> 「皇甫謐《列女傳》曰：酒泉烈女龐娥親者，表氏龐子夏之妻，祿福趙君安之女也。君安為同縣李壽所殺」[2]

**二、报仇的经过**

她的三个弟弟本欲报仇，却都死于瘟疫，李寿因此松懈防备，还聚族庆贺：

> 「會遭災疫，三人皆死。壽聞大喜，請會宗族，共相慶賀」[2]

她暗中买刀，伺机动手：

> 「陰巿名刀，挾長持短，晝夜哀酸，志在殺壽」[2]

**三、刺杀与自首（正是问题所问的情节）**

> 「至光和二年二月上旬，以白日清時，於都亭之前，與壽相遇，便下車扣壽馬，叱之。壽驚愕，回馬欲走。娥親奮刀斫之，並傷其馬。」[3]

> 「遂拔其刀以截壽頭，持詣都亭，歸罪有司，徐步詣獄，辭顏不變。」[3]

正文的记载与此一致：

> 「白日刺壽於都亭前，訖，徐詣縣，顏色不變，曰：『父讎己報，請受戮。』」[13]

**四、禄福长尹嘉放她，后来遇赦**

> 「祿福長尹嘉解印綬縱娥，娥不肯去，遂強載還家。會赦得免，州郡嘆貴，刊石表閭。」[13]

裴注补充：尹嘉「不忍論娥親，即解印綬去官，弛法縱之」[3]；她坚持不肯逃死，说「仇塞身死，妾之明分也。治獄制刑，君之常典也。何敢貪生以枉官法？」[3]。事后：

> 「涼州刺史周洪、酒泉太守劉班等並共表上，稱其烈義，刊石立碑，顯其門閭」[1]

> 「太常弘農張奐貴尚所履，以束帛二十端禮之」[1]

**五、年份**

年份只出现在裴注所引《列女传》中："光和二年二月上旬"[3]。据年号换算，光和二年为公元 179 年。陈寿正文没有记年月，只作追述（"初"）[13]。

q: A soldier who went out and never came back was treated as a deserter, and his wife and children were made government slaves. His wife protested everywhere without success. Which Commandant of Justice eventually discovered that the soldier had been murdered for money by a man from his own camp, and who was the murderer?
reply:
**Answer:** The Commandant of Justice (廷尉) was **Gao Rou 高柔**, and the murderer was **Jiao Ziwen 焦子文**, a soldier in the same camp as the victim.

**The case (from the *Sanguozhi*, biography of Gao Rou):**

The soldier's name was **Dou Li 窦礼**, of the 護軍營 (camp of the Protector of the Army). The record says:

「頃之，護軍營士竇禮近出不還。營以為亡，表言逐捕，沒其妻盈及男女為官奴婢。盈連至州府，稱冤自訟，莫有省者。乃辭詣廷尉。」[1]
(*"Before long, Dou Li, a soldier of the Protector's camp, went out and did not return. The camp took him to have deserted, memorialized to pursue and arrest him, and confiscated his wife Ying and their sons and daughters as government slaves. Ying went repeatedly to the provincial and commandery offices, protesting her innocence and pleading her own case, but no one paid attention. So she presented her plea to the Commandant of Justice."*)

Gao Rou questioned her and asked whether her husband had any enemies or money dealings. She answered:

「夫良善，與人無讎。」…「嘗出錢與同營士焦子文，求不得。」[1]

**结论：** 查出此案的是廷尉**高柔**，凶手是与窦礼同营的士兵**焦子文**。

**事实（据《三国志》原文）：**

受害士兵叫**窦礼**，是护军营的士兵。案由如下：

「頃之，護軍營士竇禮近出不還。營以為亡，表言逐捕，沒其妻盈及男女為官奴婢。盈連至州府，稱冤自訟，莫有省者。乃辭詣廷尉。」[24-0024]

（不久，护军营士兵窦礼外出后没有回来。军营认为他逃亡，上表追捕，没收其妻盈及儿女为官奴婢。盈接连到州府称冤自讼，无人理会，于是陈词到廷尉。）

廷尉高柔问她凭什么知道丈夫不是逃亡，她回答说：

「夫良善，與人無讎。」[24-0024]

「嘗出錢與同營士焦子文，求不得。」[24-0024]

（丈夫善良，与人无仇；曾借钱给同营士兵焦子文，索要未得。）

当时焦子文正好因小事被关在狱中。高柔问话时，焦子文先否认借过钱：

「自以單貧，初不敢舉人錢物也。」[24-0024]

高柔察其神色有变，于是点破，焦子文遂认罪：

「柔察子文色動，遂曰：『汝昔舉竇禮錢，何言不邪？』子文恠知事露，應對不次。柔曰：『汝已殺禮，便宜早服。』子文於是叩頭，具首殺禮本末，埋藏處所。柔便遣吏卒，承子文辭往掘禮，即得其屍。」[24-0024]

（高柔见焦子文神色变动，说：你以前借过窦礼的钱，为何说没有？焦子文惊觉事已败露，应对失次。高柔说：你已杀了窦礼，应当早认罪。焦子文于是叩头，详供杀害窦礼的始末及埋尸地点。高柔派吏卒依其供词挖掘，当即找到窦礼的尸体。）

结案后：

「詔書復盈母子為平民。班下天下，以禮為戒。」[24-0024]

（诏书免除盈母子的奴婢身份，恢复为平民；并颁下天下，以窦礼之事为戒。）

**推断：**

据上述事实——窦礼曾借钱给同营的焦子文而索讨未得，焦子文又自首杀害窦礼并供出埋尸之处——据此推断，此案与这笔债务有关；但原文并未明写焦子文行凶的动机是为钱财，只记了借钱、索讨未得与杀人自首这几件事，故动机只能说是推断，不能当作原文记载。

**关于问题里的说法：** 《三国志》原文没有直接写"为财杀人"，只记载了借钱、讨钱未得与焦子文自首杀人这几件事，是否因财起意，如上所述只能由这些事实推断。

q: In the first year of Huangwu, the Wu fleet ran into a great storm at Dongkou and many ships capsized. Men in the water clung to the big ships and cried for help, but the other ships pushed them off with halberds and spears. Who ordered that those in the water be hauled aboard, and how many were saved?
reply:
**Conclusion: Wu Can (吾粲) and Huang Yuan (黃淵) — the two of them together — gave the order to take the men aboard, and the number they saved was over a hundred.**

**Evidence**

The event is recorded in Wu Can's biography (Wu shu). The passage reads:

「黃武元年，與呂范、賀齊等俱以舟師拒魏將曹休於洞口。值天大風，諸船綆紲斷絕，漂沒著岸，為魏軍所獲，或覆沒沉溺，其大船尚存者，水中生人皆攀緣號呼，他吏士恐船傾沒，皆以戈矛撞擊不受。粲與黃淵獨令船人以承取之，左右以為船重必敗。」[1]

「粲、淵所活者百餘人。」[1]

English rendering of the key points: In the first year of Huangwu, Wu Can, together with Lü Fan, He Qi and others, used the naval force to resist the Wei general Cao Xiu at Dongkou. A great storm arose; the ships' cables snapped, some drifted and sank, some were taken by the Wei army. On the large ships that survived, the living men in the water all clung to the hulls and cried out, but the other officers and men, fearing the ships would capsize, all struck at them with halberds and spears and would not receive them. Only Wu Can and Huang Yuan ordered the boatmen to take them up; those around them thought the ships would be too heavy and would certainly founder. The men Wu Can and Huang Yuan saved were over a hundred.

- **Who gave the order:** Wu Can (吾粲) and Huang Yuan (黃淵) — 「粲與黃淵獨令船人以承取之」[1].
- **How many were saved:** over a hundred — 「粲、淵所活者百餘人」[1].
- Wu Can's style name was Kongxiu: 「吾粲字孔休，吳郡烏程人也」[21].
- The year: Huangwu 1 corresponds to 222 AD (per the era conversion tool).

**Related records found**

- He Qi's biography gives the scale of the disaster: 「會洞口諸軍遭風流溺，所亡中分」[2] — the various forces at Dongkou met the wind and were drowned, losing half their number.
- Sun Quan's annals record the campaign: 「秋九月，魏乃命曹休、張遼、臧霸出洞口，曹仁出濡須，曹眞、夏侯尚、張郃、徐晃圍南郡。權遣呂範等督五軍，以舟軍拒休等，諸葛瑾、潘璋、楊粲救南郡，朱桓以濡須督拒仁。」[10].

**Inference**

- A who-lookup for Huang Yuan (黃淵) returned no entry in the alias table, and the only place he appears in the materials I retrieved is this same passage [1]. Based on that search result (not on the text of the *Sanguozhi* itself), I cannot cite any further record about him; this is a limit of what was found, not a claim that no such record exists.

q: An official of Shu-Han dreamed that a mulberry tree grew out of a well. The dream interpreter told him he would not live past forty-eight, and sure enough he died at forty-eight. Who was this official, and who interpreted the dream?
reply:
**The official was He Zhi 何祗 (style name Junzhu 君肃); the dream interpreter was Zhao Zhi 赵直.**

The story comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary (裴注) to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, Shu book, juan 11 (the joint biographies including Yang Hong), in the portion on Yang Hong and He Zhi, where Pei quotes the *Yibu Qijiu Zhuan Zaji* 益部耆旧传杂记 [1][17].

**Who He Zhi was**

In Chen Shou's main text he appears only briefly: 「洪迎門下書佐何祗，有才策功干，舉郡吏，數年為廣漢太守，時洪亦尚在蜀郡。」[18] — Yang Hong took him in as his 門下書佐 (a clerical officer); he had talent and administrative ability, was promoted to 郡吏, and within a few years became Grand Administrator (太守) of Guanghan.

The commentary gives more of his career: 「初仕郡，後為督軍從事」, then 「出補成都令，時郫縣令缺，以祗兼二縣」; when the Yi of Wenshan were unsettled, 「以祗為汶山太守」, and afterwards 「遷廣漢」[1]; finally 「轉祗為犍為」[17].

**The dream and the prophecy**

「尝梦井中生桑，以问占梦赵直，直曰：“桑非井中之物，会当移植；然桑字四十下八，君寿恐不过此。”祗笑言“得此足矣”。」[1]

(He once dreamed that a mulberry tree grew in a well, and asked the dream interpreter Zhao Zhi about it. Zhi said: "The mulberry is not a thing that belongs in a well; it will surely be transplanted. Moreover, the character *sang* 桑 is 四十下八 — I fear your lifespan will not exceed this." He Zhi laughed and said, "To get that much is enough.")

**The fulfillment**

「转祗为犍为。年四十八卒，如直所言。」[17] — He Zhi was transferred to Jianwei; he died at forty-eight, just as Zhi had said.

**How the prediction was read**

The source itself supplies the link: Zhao Zhi read the character 桑 as 「四十下八」, and He Zhi's death at 四十八 is stated to be 「如直所言」[1][17]. 据此推断, Zhao Zhi was drawing the number forty-eight out of the written form of the character 桑 — i.e., a reading based on the graph rather than on anything that happened in the dream. The source states no more than 「桑字四十下八」; it does not say what the first half of the interpretation (「桑非井中之物，會當移植」) was taken to foretell.

**Note on the sources**

He Zhi has no biography of his own; the dream episode is not in Chen Shou's main text but in the *Yibu Qijiu Zhuan Zaji* quoted by Pei Songzhi [1][17]. The main text records only that Yang Hong took He Zhi in as his 門下書佐 and that he became Grand Administrator of Guanghan [18]. q: One of Cao Cao's military-planning officers (junmou yuan) ran into Cao Zhi on a muddy road inside the palace gate at Ye after a rain. He neither made way nor saluted, and even argued with Cao Zhi that 'the king's envoy, however lowly, ranks above the feudal lords.' Who was he, and what did he later gain from this?
reply:
**The man was Han Xuan (韓宣), courtesy name Jingran (景然), of Bohai.** He was serving as a **military-planning officer (軍謀掾) under the Chancellor (丞相)** — i.e. under Cao Cao — and was idling about at Ye (鄴). The whole episode is preserved in Pei Songzhi's commentary to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, quoting the *Weilüe* (《魏略》), attached to the biography of Pei Qian.

**What happened**

The account in Pei's commentary: 「韓宣字景然，勃海人也。爲人短小。建安中，丞相召署軍謀掾，宂散在鄴。嘗於鄴出入宮，於東掖門內與臨菑侯植相遇。時天新雨，地有泥潦。宣欲避之，閡潦不得去。乃以扇自障，住於道邊。」[11] — Han Xuan, a short man, was appointed military-planning officer in the Jian'an period and was idling at Ye; one day he met the Marquis of Linzi, Cao Zhi, inside the eastern side gate just after rain, with mud and standing water on the ground; he wanted to step aside but was blocked by the water, so he covered himself with a fan and stood by the roadside.

He did not salute, and when Cao Zhi stopped his carriage and sent an attendant to ask what office he held, the exchange ran: 「宣云：『丞相軍謀掾也。』植又問曰：『應得唐突列侯否？』宣曰：『春秋之義，王人雖微，列于諸侯之上，未聞宰士而爲下士諸侯禮也。』」[6] — Xuan said he was the Chancellor's military-planning officer; Zhi asked whether he was entitled to be so rude to a marquis; Xuan replied that by the *Spring and Autumn* principle the king's envoy, however lowly, ranks above the feudal lords, and he had never heard of a subordinate official having to pay the rites of an inferior to a marquis.

Zhi pressed him again: 「植又曰：『即如所言，爲人父吏，見其子應有禮否？』宣又曰：『於禮，臣、子一例也，而宣年又長。』植知其枝柱難窮，乃釋去，具爲太子言，以爲辯。」[6] — Zhi argued that if so, a servant of the father ought at least to show propriety to the son; Xuan answered that in ritual, subject and son are treated as one category, and he was older besides. Zhi saw he could not be cornered and let him go, then **reported the whole thing to the Heir Apparent (太子) — that is, Cao Pi — commending Xuan as a man of argument.**

**What he gained from it**

This is exactly where the payoff comes. In the Huangchu period Han Xuan was **Secretariat Gentleman (尚書郎)**, and once, when he was due to be punished in front of the hall, already bound with the rods not yet applied, Emperor Wen (Cao Pi) passed by in his carriage: 「帝追念前臨菑侯所說，乃寤曰：『是子建所道韓宣邪！』特原之，遂解其縛。」[6] — the emperor recalled what the Marquis of Linzi had once said, realised this was the Han Xuan "Zijian spoke of," and **specially pardoned him and had him untied.** So what he gained from the encounter was, first, Cao Zhi's recommendation to Cao Pi for his eloquence, and years later, on the strength of that remembered recommendation, an imperial pardon from Cao Pi himself.

His later career: 「後出爲清河、東郡太守。明帝時，爲尚書大鴻臚，數歲卒。宣前後當官，在能否之間，然善以己恕人。」[6] — he went out as Administrator (太守) of Qinghe and Dong commanderies; under Emperor Ming he served as **Director of the Secretariat (尚書) and Grand Herald (大鴻臚)**, dying some years later; as an official he was mediocre in competence, but good at forgiving others by putting himself in their place.

One further note from the commentary: Pei Songzhi observes 「案本志，宣名都不見，惟《魏略》有此傳，而《世語》列於名臣之流」[22] — Han Xuan's name does not appear anywhere in Chen Shou's main text; only the *Weilüe* has this biography of him, while the *Shiyu* places him among the famous officials.

So, to summarise: the officer was **Han Xuan, styled Jingran**, a Chancellor's military-planning officer; the row at the eastern side gate of the Ye palace, in which he refused to yield or salute and invoked the principle that the king's envoy outranks the feudal lords, was reported by Cao Zhi to Cao Pi as proof of his debating skill — and that very report later earned him a pardon from Emperor Wen when he stood bound for punishment as a Secretariat Gentleman.

review_raw:
**结论：此人是韩宣，字景然，勃海人**，当时任丞相军谋掾，闲散在邺城。他从这件事上得到的好处是：曹植把这场应对原原本本告诉了太子，称赞他善辩；到黄初年间他做尚书郎、因职事要在殿前受罚、已被捆绑时，魏文帝想起当年临菑侯说过的这番话，特意赦免了他，解开捆绑。

**一、事实（原文依据）**

他的身份与相遇的经过，裴注引《魏略》记：「韓宣字景然，勃海人也。爲人短小。建安中，丞相召署軍謀掾，宂散在鄴。嘗於鄴出入宮，於東掖門內與臨菑侯植相遇。時天新雨，地有泥潦。宣欲避之，閡潦不得去。乃以扇自障，住於道邊。」[11]

曹植的嫌恶与盘问：「植嫌宣既不去，又不爲禮，乃駐車，使其常從問宣何官？宣云：『丞相軍謀掾也。』植又問曰：『應得唐突列侯否？』宣曰：『春秋之義，王人雖微，列于諸侯之上，未聞宰士而爲下士諸侯禮也。』」[6]

两人的继续争辩与曹植的反应：「植又曰：『即如所言，爲人父吏，見其子應有禮否？』宣又曰：『於禮，臣、子一例也，而宣年又長。』植知其枝柱難窮，乃釋去，具爲太子言，以爲辯。」[6]

后来的结果：「黃初中，爲尚書郎，嘗以職事當受罰於殿前，已縛，束杖未行。文帝輦過，問：『此爲誰？』左右對曰：『尚書郎勃海韓宣也。』帝追念前臨菑侯所說，乃寤曰：『是子建所道韓宣邪！』特原之，遂解其縛。」[6]

此后的仕历：「後出爲清河、東郡太守。明帝時，爲尚書大鴻臚，數歲卒。宣前後當官，在能否之間，然善以己恕人。」[6]

这段记载的出处与流传情况：它是裴注所引《魏略》，裴松之按：「案本志，宣名都不見，惟《魏略》有此傳，而《世語》列於名臣之流。」[22]

**二、推断**

- 韩宣所事的"丞相"是谁：资料只写「丞相召署軍謀掾」，没有写出姓名。曹植在建安年间为临菑侯，其父即《陈思王曹植传》中的"太祖"，传中记「太祖征孫權，使植留守鄴」[1]。据此推断，此处的"丞相"即曹操。
- "太子"是谁：原文只说曹植「具爲太子言」，没有点明太子是谁；但下文记文帝（曹丕）「追念前臨菑侯所說」[6]，据此推断这位太子就是后来的魏文帝曹丕。
- 时间先后：相遇记在「建安中」，受罚与获赦记在「黃初中」[6]。据此推断赦免发生在相遇之后。原文没有给相遇的具体年份，也没有说两事相隔多久，所以只能说到"先后"，不能说到具体年数。
- 获赦的原因：原文写文帝「追念前臨菑侯所說，乃寤曰……特原之」[6]，据此推断他这次获赦与曹植当年在太子面前称许他善辩直接相关。不过原文只记文帝"追念"而"特原之"，是否另有别的原因，资料没有交代，不能断定这是唯一原因。
- 他所"得到"的：综合上两条事实——曹植「具爲太子言，以爲辯」[6]，以及后来文帝凭这段记忆赦免他[6]——据此推断，他在这件事上得到的是曹植向太子的一次称许，以及多年后由此而来的一次赦免。

**三、余论**

韩宣此人不见于陈寿正文，其事迹仅靠《魏略》保存，裴松之也指出「案本志，宣名都不見」[22]。

q: A man opened up wasteland at Yongxing and planted twenty-odd mu of rice. Just as it was ripening, a local claimed it as his own; the man simply let him have the rice, and when the county Chief wanted to punish the local, he even pleaded on his behalf. Who was this man?
reply:

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
In the *Sanguozhi*, **two** men had the courtesy name **Wenze (文則)**:

1. **Yu Jin (于禁)**, a Wei general. His biography opens: 「于禁字文則，泰山鉅平人也。」[1] — "Yu Jin, courtesy name Wenze, was a man of Juping in Taishan commandery." He first followed Bao Xin during the Yellow Turban rising, later joined Cao Cao (then acting as Governor of Yan province) and rose through campaigns against Lü Bu, Zhang Xiu, and others, being enfeoffed as Marquis of Yishou Pavilion [2].

2. **Wu Fan (吳範)**, a Wu official and diviner. His biography opens: 「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也。」[3] — "Wu Fan, courtesy name Wenze, was a man of Shangyu in Kuaiji commandery." He was known in his commandery for calendrical reckoning and reading the winds, was recommended as a "Possessor of the Way" (有道), and after Sun Quan rose in the southeast he served him, his prognostications usually proving accurate [3].

So the question "who had the courtesy name Wenze?" has no single answer: one is the Wei general **Yu Jin**, the other the Wu diviner **Wu Fan**. If you have another clue (which state he served, what office he held, what event he was involved in), I can tell you which one is meant.

q: The Weilüe mentions a man called 'Nukou' ('Slave Bandit'). Who was he, and which other generals' alternative names are given in the same passage?
reply:
## Conclusion

"Nukou" (奴寇) was an alternative name of **Zang Ba** (臧霸). The same passage of the *Weilüe* also gives the alternative names of **Sun Guan** (孫觀) — "Yingzi" (嬰子), **Wu Dun** (吳敦) — "Annu" (黯奴), and **Yin Li** (尹禮) — "Lu'er" (盧兒).

## Evidence

The passage is Pei Songzhi's annotation to the Zang Ba biography, quoting the *Weilüe*:

「《魏略》曰：霸一名奴寇。孫觀名嬰子。吳敦名黯奴。尹禮名盧兒。」[1]

(*Weilüe*: "Ba had one other name, Nukou. Sun Guan's name was Yingzi. Wu Dun's name was Annu. Yin Li's name was Lu'er.")

So "Nukou" is not a separate person but Zang Ba's second name; Pei Songzhi quotes this from the *Weilüe*.

Zang Ba, styled Xuangao, was a man of Huaxian in Taishan Commandery:

「臧霸字宣高，泰山華人也。」[25]

When the Yellow Turbans rose, he followed Tao Qian to defeat them and was appointed Commandant of Cavalry:

「黃巾起，霸從陶謙擊破之，拜騎都尉。」[25]

He then gathered troops in Xu Province together with Sun Guan, Wu Dun, Yin Li and others, with himself as their leader, encamped at Kaiyang:

「遂收兵於徐州，與孫觀、吳敦、尹禮等並聚眾，霸為帥，屯於開陽。」[25]

When Taizu (太祖) attacked Lü Bu, Zang Ba and the others brought troops to aid Lü Bu:

「太祖之討呂布也，霸等將兵助布。」[25]

After Lü Bu was captured, Zang Ba hid himself:

「既禽布，霸自匿。」[25]

Taizu sought him out and, pleased with him, had him summon the others, and appointed them:

「太祖募索得霸，見而悅之，使霸招吳敦、尹禮、孫觀、觀兄康等，皆詣太祖。」[25]

「太祖以霸為琅邪相，敦利城、禮東莞、觀北海、康城陽太守」[25]

(*Taizu made Ba Chancellor of Langye; Dun [Administrator of] Licheng, Li [Administrator of] Dongguan, Guan [Administrator of] Beihai, Kang [Administrator of] Chengyang.*)

The same *Weilüe* passage also records their later history under Wei:

「建安二十四年，霸遣別軍在洛。會太祖崩，霸所部及青州兵，以為天下將亂，皆鳴鼓擅去。」[1]

(*In the 24th year of Jian'an, Ba sent a detached force to station at Luo. Meeting with Taizu's death, Ba's troops and the Qingzhou troops, thinking the realm would fall into chaos, all beat drums and departed without orders.*)

And that Emperor Wen (文帝) took his troops from him:

「遂東巡，因霸來朝而奪其兵。」[1]

(*He then toured east, and took advantage of Ba's coming to court to seize his troops.*)

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
**Conclusion: Wang Fan (王蕃), courtesy name Yongyuan (永元). The year given by his biography is the second year of Sun Wu's Ganlu 甘露 era = 266 CE.**

**The person and the event**

Wang Fan was a man of Lujiang commandery: 「王蕃字永元，廬江人也。」[16]. He had earlier held the office in question — Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant (散騎中常侍) — under Sun Xiu: 「孫休即位，與賀邵、薛瑩、虞汜俱為散騎中常侍，皆加駙馬都尉。」[16]. Under Sun Hao he re-entered court as a Regular Palace Attendant (常侍): 「孫皓初。復入為常侍，與萬彧同官。」[4]. Lu Kai's memorial likewise calls him 「常侍王蕃」[21].

The banquet incident, in the biography of Wang Fan:

「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。皓疑而不悅，舉蕃出外。頃之請還，酒亦不解。蕃性有威嚴，行止自若，皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之。衛將軍滕牧、征西將軍留平請，不能得。」[1]

("In the second year of Ganlu, when Ding Zhong returned from his embassy to Jin, Sun Hao held a great assembly of his ministers. Wang Fan, dead drunk, collapsed. Sun Hao grew suspicious and displeased and had Wang Fan carried out. After a while he asked to return; his drunkenness had still not worn off. Wang Fan was by nature dignified and bore himself as usual. Sun Hao flew into a rage and shouted to his attendants to behead him below the hall. The General of the Guard Teng Mu and the General Who Conquers the West Liu Ping pleaded for him, but could not obtain a pardon.")

The embassy that preceded it is recorded in Sun Hao's annals: 「寶鼎元年正月，遣大鴻臚張儼、五官中郎將丁忠弔祭晉文帝。及還，儼道病死。」[9] ("In the first month of the first year of Baoding, he sent the Grand Herald Zhang Yan and the Commandant of the Gentlemen of the Household Ding Zhong to offer condolences on the death of Emperor Wen of Jin. On the return, Zhang Yan died of illness on the road.")

**The year**

The biography dates the killing to 「甘露二年」[1]; Sun Wu's Ganlu 2nd year = **266 CE** (era tool).

**A divergent version in Pei Songzhi's commentary**

The commentary preserves other accounts and marks the conflict. 裴注引《江表傳》: 「皓用巫史之言，谓建业宫不利，乃西巡武昌，仍有迁都之意，恐群臣不从，乃大请会，赐将吏」[5], and in that version Sun Hao kills Wang Fan at the hall after asking him the meaning of an Ode line; the commentary adds 「此與本傳不同」[5]. 裴注引《吳錄》: 「皓每於会，因酒酣，辄令侍臣嘲谑公卿，以为笑乐」[5], and records Wang Fan's mocking of Wan Yu at a time when Wan Yu was already Left Chancellor [5]. Pei Songzhi's own verdict: 「臣松之按本传云丁忠使晋还，皓为大会，於会中杀蕃，检忠从北还在此年之春，彧时尚未为丞相，至秋乃为相耳。吴录所言为乖互不同。」[5]. The biography adds that Wang Fan died at thirty-nine and that Sun Hao deported his family to Guangzhou: 「蕃死時年三十九，皓徙蕃家屬廣州」[21], and Lu Kai's memorial lamented him as 「斯社稷之重鎮，大吳之龍逢也」[21].

**Inference (据此推断)**

The facts available are: (i) the biography's wording 「丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣」[1] — the embassy's return, then the assembly; (ii) the annals' record of the dispatch 「寶鼎元年正月」[9]; (iii) Pei Songzhi's remark 「檢忠從北還在此年之春」[5]. From (i) it follows that the banquet came after Ding Zhong's return — this order is stated in the text, not merely presumed. From (ii) and (iii) it follows that the annals and the commentary date the embassy's dispatch and return under different era years, and that Pei Songzhi places the return in the spring of the year of the killing; since the sources label the years differently, both datings should be reported side by side rather than merged into one. The sources do not say why Sun Hao ordered the killing; nothing here supports a causal claim beyond what each version states.

q: Who was the man that Kuan Yü's troops called the 'White Horse General' (Baima jiangjun)?
reply:
**Conclusion: the "White Horse General" was Pang De (龐德), style Lingming (令明).**

**Evidence**

His biography in the *Wei shu* (the section on Pang De) introduces him as 「龐德字令明，南安狟道人也」[1] — "Pang De, style Lingming, a man of Huandao in Nan'an."

He first served under Ma Teng against the rebel Qiang and Di, and later, following Ma Teng's son Ma Chao, fought Guo Yuan and Gao Gan at Pingyang as the army's vanguard, 「親斬援首」[1] — "he personally cut off Guo Yuan's head." After Cao Cao pacified Hanzhong, 「太祖定漢中，德隨眾降。太祖素聞其驍勇，拜立義將軍，封關門亭侯，邑三百戶」[1] — "Taizu pacified Hanzhong, and Pang De surrendered with the others. Taizu had long heard of his ferocity and courage, and appointed him General of Righteousness Established (立義將軍), enfeoffing him as Marquis of the Guannen Pavilion (關門亭侯) with 300 households."

The nickname itself: 「後親與羽交戰，射羽中額。時德常乘白馬，羽軍謂之白馬將軍，皆憚之」[3] — "Later he fought Guan Yu in person and shot Guan Yu in the forehead. At that time Pang De always rode a white horse; Guan Yu's troops called him the White Horse General, and all dreaded him."

Before the fighting, the generals at Fan suspected him because his brother was in Hanzhong: 「討關羽，樊下諸將以德兄在漢中，頗疑之」[3] — "When Guan Yu was to be attacked, the generals at Fan rather suspected him because his brother was in Hanzhong." Pei Songzhi's note quotes the *Wei lue*: 「德從兄名柔，時在蜀」[9] — "Pang De's elder cousin was named Pang Rou and was then in Shu." Pang De answered the suspicion with 「我受國恩，義在效死。我欲身自擊羽。今年我不殺羽，羽當殺我」[3] — "I have received the state's favor, and by right I should die for it. I want to strike Guan Yu myself. If I do not kill Guan Yu this year, Guan Yu will kill me."

The flood and the campaign: 「會天霖雨十餘日，漢水暴溢」[3] — "It happened that it rained heavily for more than ten days, and the Han River violently overflowed." Yu Jin's biography gives the campaign: 「建安二十四年，太祖在長安，使曹仁討關羽於樊，又遣禁助仁。秋，大霖雨，漢水溢，平地水數丈，禁等七軍皆沒」[6] — "In the twenty-fourth year of Jian'an, Taizu was in Chang'an and sent Cao Ren to attack Guan Yu at Fan, and also sent Yu Jin to aid Cao Ren. q: Who was the Marquis of Panyu, and for what achievement was he given that title?
reply:
**Conclusion:** The Marquis of Panyu (番禺侯) was **Lü Dai** (呂岱, style Dinggong 定公), a general who served Sun Quan. He received the title as a reward for crushing the resistance of **Shi Hui** (士徽) — son of the Jiaozhi Grand Administrator Shi Xie — in Jiao province, and for defeating Shi Hui's generals afterwards.

**Evidence (Lü Dai's biography, Wu shu):**

- His identity and origin: 「呂岱字定公，廣陵海陵人也，為郡縣吏，避亂南渡。孫權統事，岱詣幕府」[2].
- He already held a fief before Panyu. The passage opens 「延康元年，代步騭為交州刺史」, and in the same passage records 「遷安南將軍，假節，封都鄉侯」[4]. (The year 延康元年 is given for his succeeding Bu Zhi as Inspector of Jiao province; the promotion and the Duxiang fief are recorded in the same passage without a separate date.)
- The occasion: 「交阯太守士燮卒，權以燮子徽為安遠將軍，領九真太守」[1]; Lü Dai memorialized to divide the southern commanderies, and when Shi Hui would not accept the order, 「舉兵戍海口以拒良等」[1]. Lü Dai then 「上疏請討徽罪，督兵三千人晨夜浮海」, and 「遂行，過合浦，與良俱進」[1].
- The grant of the title follows directly on the killing of Shi Hui and the rout of his generals: 「徽聞岱至，果大震怖，不知所出，即率兄弟六人肉袒迎岱。岱皆斬送其首，徽大將甘醴，桓治等率吏民攻岱，岱奮擊大破之，進封番禺侯」[1].
- Shi Xie's biography gives the same affair in more detail, including the ruse: Shi Kuang (士匡), son of Shi Yi, 「與岱有舊，岱署匡師友從事，先移書交阯，告喻禍福，又遣匡見徽，說令服罪，雖失郡守，保無他憂」, and then 「岱起，擁節讀詔書，數徵罪過，左右因反縛以出，即皆伏誅，傳首詣武昌」[8].
- The sequel: 「岱既定交州，復進討九真，斬獲以萬數。又遣從事南宣國化，暨徼外扶南、林邑、堂明諸王，各遣使奉貢。權嘉其功，進拜鎮南將軍」[1].

**Inference (my own reasoning, on this evidence):** The fief was given for the pacification of Jiao province, i.e. the destruction of Shi Hui's resistance and the re-establishment of Wu's hold there. My grounds are: (a) the text places 「進封番禺侯」 immediately after the killing of Shi Hui and the defeat of Gan Li and Huan Zhi [1]; (b) the further campaigns against Jiuzhen and the tribute missions of Funan, Linyi and Tangming are recorded only afterwards, together with the separate promotion to General Who Guards the South [1]; (c) his earlier, different fief was the Marquisate of Duxiang [4]. From these it follows that the Panyu title was attached to the Jiao-province settlement, not to an earlier exploit — but note that neither source states the year of the enfeoffment itself. Shi Xie is said to have died in the fifth year of Huang-wu (「燮在郡四十餘歲，黃武五年，年九十卒」[14]), while Lü Dai's own biography records the affair without a year, so I do not attach a year to the Panyu fief.

**Note on a different Panyu mention:** Panyu also appears in Xue Zong's memorial in an unrelated, much earlier context: 「趙佗起番禺，懷服百越之君」[10] — this refers to Zhao Tuo in the Qin–Han period, not to the Wu marquisate.

**Differing judgement in the commentary:** Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting Sun Sheng condemns Lü Dai over this very act: 「吕岱师友士匡，使通信誓，徽兄弟肉袒，推心委命，岱因灭之，以要功利，君子是以知孙权之不能远略，而吕氏之祚不延者也」[12] (Sun Sheng's verdict: Lü Dai used Shi Kuang to convey a sworn promise, and then destroyed the Shi brothers for profit). This is Sun Sheng's assessment, quoted by Pei Songzhi, not Chen Shou's own narrative.

q: Why was Wei Zhao put to death by Sun Hao?
reply:
## Conclusion

Wei Zhao — the text writes his name 韋曜 — was put to death by Sun Hao after a series of accumulated offenses. The text says Sun Hao 「遂積前後嫌忿，收曜付獄，是歲鳳凰二年也」[1] ("accumulated his resentments from before and after and had Wei Yao thrown into prison; that year was Fenghuang 2"), and when Hua He petitioned to spare him, 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵」[11] ("Sun Hao refused, and so executed Wei Yao, deporting a hundred families of his household to Lingling"). The imprisonment is dated by the text to Fenghuang 2, which the era conversion gives as 273 CE.

## The offenses recorded

**1. Belittling the reported auspicious signs.** The text: 「時所在承指數言瑞應。皓以問曜，曜答曰：『此人家筐篋中物耳。』」[1]

**2. Refusing to make an "Annals" (紀) for Sun He.** 「又皓欲為父和作紀，曜執以和不登帝位，宜名為傳。如是者非一，漸見責怒。」[1]

**3. The drinking-party offenses.** Sun Hao's banquets were all-day affairs with a seven-sheng quota: 「皓每饗宴，無不竟日，坐席無能否率以七升為限」[1]. Wei Yao 「曜素飲酒不過二升」[1], and once his favor declined, 「至於寵衰，更見逼強，輒以為罪」[1]. He also declined to join the practice of humiliating officials: 「故但示難問經義言論而已」[1]. Sun Hao took this as disobedience: 「皓以為不承用詔命，意不忠盡」[1].

**4. The "soiled manuscript" affair.** While in prison Wei Yao submitted a memorial listing his unfinished scholarly works, including 《洞紀》 and 《官職訓》《辯釋名》[17]. Sun Hao instead 「皓更怪其書之垢故，又以詰曜」[13], and Wei Yao's abject reply, 「謹追辭叩頭五百下，兩手自搏」[13], did not save him.

**5. Hua He's petition was refused.** Hua He's memorial pleading for him includes: 「曜年已七十，餘數無幾，乞赦其一等之罪，為終身徒，使成書業，水足傳未，垂之百世。」[11] The outcome: 「皓不許，遂誅曜，徙百家零陵。子隆，亦有文學也。」[11]

The historian's verdict on Sun Hao fits the pattern: 「忠諫者誅，讒諛者進」[6].

## Inference

The text dates the imprisonment to Fenghuang 2 [1], then records Wei Yao's own prison memorial [17], then Hua He's petition [13], and only afterwards 「遂誅曜」[11]. 据此推断: since the execution is narrated after the petition that followed the imprisonment, the execution came at or after the Fenghuang 2 imprisonment, i.e., not earlier than 273 CE. The text does not state the execution's own date.

q: What is the story of Kuan Yü killing Ts'ai Yang at Ku-ch'eng?
reply:
## Short answer

The story of Guan Yu (Kuan Yü) killing Cai Yang (Ts'ai Yang) at Gucheng (Ku-ch'eng) is **a Romance of the Three Kingdoms episode, not a Sanguozhi one**. In the *Sanguozhi* there is no Gucheng meeting and no killing of Cai Yang by Guan Yu. What the *Sanguozhi* does record is (1) that Guan Yu left Cao Cao and went back to Liu Bei, and (2) that Cai Yang was sent by Cao Cao against Liu Bei in Runan and was **killed by Liu Bei** (or, in a variant account, defeated by the bandit Gong Du). Guan Yu is not credited with it anywhere.

## What the *Sanguozhi* actually says

**Guan Yu did leave Cao Cao to rejoin Liu Bei** — this part is in the biography of Guan Yu [1]:
> 「羽盡封其所賜，拜書告辭，而奔先主於袁軍。左右欲追之，曹公曰：『彼各為其主，勿追也。』」
(Guan Yu sealed up all the gifts he had received, sent a letter of farewell, and fled to Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's army. Cao Cao's attendants wanted to pursue him; Cao Cao said, "Each man serves his own lord — do not pursue.")

**Cai Yang's end, in the biography of Liu Bei (Xianzhu)** [2]:
> 「紹遣先主將本兵復至汝南，與賊龔都等合，眾數千人。曹公遣蔡陽擊之，為先主所殺。」
(Yuan Shao sent the Xianzhu with his own troops back to Runan, where he joined the bandit Gong Du and others, several thousand strong. Cao Cao sent Cai Yang to attack them, and Cai Yang was killed by the Xianzhu.)

So here the killer is **Liu Bei**, and the place is **Runan** — not Gucheng, and not Guan Yu.

**The same affair, in the Annals of Emperor Wu (Wudi ji)** [35], differs on both the name and the outcome:
> 「紹之未破也，使劉備略汝南，汝南賊共都等應之。遣蔡揚擊都，不利，爲都所破。」
(Before Yuan Shao was defeated, he sent Liu Bei to raid Runan; the Runan bandit Gong Du and others responded to him. [Cao Cao] sent Cai Yang [written 蔡揚] to attack Gong Du, but he was unsuccessful and was beaten by Gong Du.)

## Points worth noting

- The two accounts of Cai Yang's defeat disagree: the *Xianzhu* biography says he was **killed by Liu Bei**; the *Wudi ji* says he was **beaten by Gong Du**. They also spell the name differently (蔡陽 vs. 蔡揚). The *Sanguozhi* itself does not reconcile them, so both should be reported as they stand rather than picked as the single truth.
- Guan Yu's own biography [1] records only that he fled back to Liu Bei in Yuan Shao's army; it says nothing about him encountering Cai Yang.

**Inference (drawn from the above, not a record):** Since the *Sanguozhi* places Cai Yang's defeat in Runan and attributes it to Liu Bei (or to Gong Du), and since it nowhere has Guan Yu fighting Cai Yang, the *Sanguozhi* gives no support for a Guan-Yu-kills-Cai-Yang story. That story belongs to a later tradition.

---

*The following is not from the Sanguozhi:* The tale that Guan Yu, on his way back to Liu Bei, met Zhang Fei at Gucheng and there killed the pursuing Cai Yang is the *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* version (part of the "passing five passes and slaying six generals" cycle); the *Sanguozhi* has no such episode. Gucheng (古城) here is the name used in the novel; it is not the place of Cai Yang's death in the histories.

**一、关羽确实离开曹操、回到刘备那里**，见《关羽传》[1]：

## Conclusion

The premise of the question does not match the sources. In the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国志》), the ruse at Bowang was **not** Zhuge Liang's plan and was **not** a fire attack that burned Xiahou Dun's army. It was carried out by **Liu Bei himself**, and the fire was the burning of his *own* camp as a feigned flight to draw the enemy into a prepared ambush:

> 「久之，先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁，惇等追之，為伏兵所破。」[1]

(*After a long while, the Prior Lord set an ambush; one morning he burned his own camp and pretended to flee. Dun and the others pursued him, and were broken by the ambush force.*)

## Evidence from the sources

**1. Liu Bei is the actor; the burned camp was his own.**

The *Xianzhu zhuan* (先主傳) gives the whole sequence [1]:

> 「曹公既破紹，自南擊先主。先主遣麋竺、孫乾與劉表相聞，表自郊迎，以上賓禮待之，益其兵，使屯新野。」[1]

(*After Duke Cao broke Shao, he turned south to attack the Prior Lord. The Prior Lord sent Mi Zhu and Sun Qian to make contact with Liu Biao; Biao received him in person outside the city, treated him with the courtesy due an honored guest, reinforced his troops, and settled him at Xinye.*)

> 「使拒夏侯惇、于禁等於博望。」[1]

(*He was made to resist Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin and others at Bowang.*)

The ruse itself is the sentence quoted in the conclusion: the phrase 「自燒屯」 makes clear he burned *his own* camp, so this was a deception, not a fire attack consuming the enemy.

**2. Li Dian's biography records the same event, naming the Wei commanders and describing the ground.**

> 「劉表使劉備北侵，至葉，太祖遣典從夏侯惇拒之。備一旦燒屯去，惇率諸軍追擊之」[37]

(*Liu Biao sent Liu Bei to invade northward; when he reached Ye, the Grand Ancestor sent Dian to follow Xiahou Dun and resist him. One morning Bei burned his camp and left; Dun led the armies in pursuit...*)

Li Dian warned against pursuit:

> 「賊無故退，疑必有伏。南道狹窄，草木深，不可追也。」[37]

(*The bandits withdraw without cause; I suspect there must be an ambush. The southern road is narrow and the vegetation is deep; we must not pursue.*)

> 「惇不聽，與於禁追之，典留守。惇等果入賊伏里，戰不利，典往救，備望見救至，乃散退。」[37]

(*Dun did not heed him, and with Yu Jin pursued, while Dian stayed to guard. Dun and the others indeed entered the bandits' ambush, and the battle went badly; Dian went to the rescue, and Bei, seeing the relief arrive, dispersed and withdrew.*)

So the Wei officers named are **Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin, and Li Dian** (Li Dian remaining as the reserve), and the ambush ground is described as a narrow road with deep vegetation.

**3. No source retrieved connects Zhuge Liang with Bowang.**

I found no record of Zhuge Liang at Bowang. His biography's earliest account of his dealings with Liu Bei is the meeting at the thatched hut and then the mission to Sun Quan:

> 「時左將軍劉備以亮有殊量，乃三顧亮於草廬之中」[24]

(*At that time the General of the Left, Liu Bei, considered Liang to have extraordinary capacity, and so visited Liang three times in the thatched hut.*)

> 「亮時年二十七，乃建奇策，身使孫權，求援吳會。」[24]

(*Liang was then twenty-seven years old; he devised a remarkable plan, went in person to Sun Quan, and sought aid from Wu.*)

There is, however, a competing account of the first meeting. Pei Songzhi's note quotes 《魏略》:

> 「亮乃北行見備」[34]

(*Liang then went north to see Bei.*)

Pei Songzhi rejects this, citing the *Chu shi biao*:

> 「臣松之以為亮表云『先帝不以臣卑鄙，猥自枉屈，三顧臣於草廬之中，諮臣以當世之事』，則非亮先詣備，明矣。」[32]

(*Pei Songzhi's note: Liang's memorial says, "The late Emperor did not consider me base and mean, but humbled himself and visited me three times in the thatched hut, consulting me on the affairs of the age." Then it is clear that Liang did not first go to Bei.*)

From the facts above — (a) the text of the *Xianzhu zhuan* attributes the stratagem directly to Liu Bei: 「先主設伏兵，一旦自燒屯偽遁」[1]; (b) Li Dian's biography likewise says 「備一旦燒屯去」[37] — it follows, 据此推断, that the burning-camp ambush at Bowang was Liu Bei's own device, not Zhuge Liang's.

On whether Zhuge Liang could have been present: Pei Songzhi dates the first meeting of the two men as follows:

> 「臣松之案：劉備以建安十三年敗，遣亮使吳，亮以建興五年抗表北伐，自傾覆至此整二十年。然則備始與亮相遇，在敗軍之前一年時也。」[41]

(*Pei Songzhi's note: Liu Bei was defeated in Jian'an 13 and sent Liang on a mission to Wu; Liang submitted his memorial for the northern campaign in Jianxing 5, exactly twenty years from that collapse to this. Thus Bei first encountered Liang one year before the defeat of his army.*)

据此推断, the first meeting falls one year before the Jian'an 13 defeat, i.e. in Jian'an 12. The retrieved passages, however, do not date the Bowang engagement itself; the *Xianzhu zhuan* only narrates it after Cao Cao's defeat of Yuan Shao and while Liu Bei was settled at Xinye [1]. Whether the meeting preceded or followed Bowang therefore cannot be settled from these passages. But on either account the sources assign the stratagem to Liu Bei, and even the 《魏略》 version places Zhuge Liang's first meeting with Liu Bei at 樊城 (「備屯於樊城」[34]), not at Bowang.

q: Who was Zhou Tai?
reply:
The name "Zhou Tai" corresponds to **two different men** in the *Sanguozhi*, and the question does not say which is meant, so both are given.

## 1. Zhou Tai 周泰, courtesy name Youping (幼平) — Wu general

A native of Xiaocai in Jiujiang commandery, he served Sun Ce alongside Jiang Qin, and Sun Quan then asked to have him for himself:

「周泰字幼平，九江下蔡人也。與蔣欽隨孫策爲左右，服事恭敬，數戰有功。」[1]

「權愛其爲人，請以自給。」[1]

When Sun Ce was campaigning against the bandits of the six counties and Sun Quan was stationed at Xuancheng, the bandits suddenly arrived; Zhou Tai alone shielded Sun Quan and took twelve wounds:

「惟泰奮激，投身衞權，膽氣倍人，左右由泰並能就戰。賊旣解散，身被十二創，良乆乃蘇。是日無泰，權幾危殆。」[1]

For this Sun Ce rewarded him: 「策深德之，補春穀長。」[1] Earlier, when Sun Ce entered Kuaiji, he had given him a post and troops: 「策入會稽，署別部司馬，授兵。」[1]

He later fought at Red Cliffs and at Nanjun against Cao Ren, and after Cao Cao's Ruxu campaign he was left in charge of Ruxu and made 平虜將軍, though Zhu Ran and Xu Sheng, then under his command, would not submit:

「後與周瑜、程普拒曹公於赤壁，攻曹仁於南郡。」[3]

「曹公退，留督濡須，拜平虜將軍。時朱然、徐盛等皆在所部，並不伏也」[3]

Sun Quan personally showed his scars at a banquet to make them submit:

「權自行酒到泰前，命泰解衣，權手自指其創痕，問以所起。」[3]

The *Jiangbiao zhuan* (裴注引《江表傳》) records Sun Quan weeping and addressing him by his courtesy name:

「幼平，卿爲孤兄弟戰如熊虎，不惜軀命，被創數十，膚如刻畫，孤亦何心不待卿以骨肉之恩，委卿以兵馬之重乎！卿吳之功臣，孤當與卿同榮辱，等休戚。」[2]

After Sun Quan broke Guan Yu, Zhou Tai was made 漢中太守、奮威將軍 and enfeoffed as 陵陽侯, and he died during the Huangwu era:

「後權破關羽，欲進圖蜀，拜泰漢中太守、奮威將軍，封陵陽侯。黃武中卒。」[3]

His son 周邵 led troops as 騎都尉, became 裨將軍 and died in Huanglong 2; his younger brother 周承 took over the troops and inherited the marquisate:

「子邵以騎都尉領兵。曹仁出濡須，戰有功，又從攻破曹休，進位裨將軍，黃龍二年卒。弟承領兵襲侯。」[3]

## 2. Zhou Tai 州泰 — Wei general

A Nanyang man, a peer of Deng Ai, skilled at war, who reached 征虜將軍 and 假節都督江南諸軍事, and died in Jingyuan 2 (261 CE), receiving posthumous titles:

「艾州里時輩南陽州泰，亦好立功業，善用兵，官至征虜將軍、假節都督江南諸軍事。景元二年薨，追贈衛將軍，諡曰壯侯。」[12]

According to the *Shiyu* (裴注引《世語》), the Jingzhou governor Pei Qian first employed him as 從事 and repeatedly sent him to Sima Yi (司馬宣王), by whom he was noticed; after Sima Yi's campaign against Meng Da he was summoned, and after a nine-year mourning period he was promoted to Administrator of Xincheng, later serving as Inspector of Yan and Yu provinces:

「初，荊州刺史裴潛以泰為從事，司馬宣王鎮宛，潛數遣詣宣王，由此為宣王所知。及征孟達，泰又導軍，遂辟泰。泰頻喪考、妣、祖，九年居喪，宣王留缺待之，至三十六日，擢為新城太守。」[11]

「後歷兗、豫州刺史，所在有籌算績效。」[11]

He also appears in the Wu record as the Wei Inspector of Yanzhou who blocked Zhu Yi at Yangyuan, after which Zhu Yi was routed and pursued by him:

「魏兗州刺史州泰據異於陽淵，異敗退，為泰所追，死傷二干人。」[19]

**Which one is meant (inference):** The sources give two distinct men under this name, one in the Wu section and one in the Wei section. Reasoning from the facts cited above — 周泰's career is tied to Sun Ce, Sun Quan, Red Cliffs and Ruxu [1][3], while 州泰's is tied to Sima Yi, Deng Ai and the Wei campaigns [11][12][19] — it follows that if the context of the question is Sun Quan's wars, the man meant is 周泰 (Youping); if the context is Sima Yi, Deng Ai, or the Wei campaigns, it is 州泰. The question as put gives no such context, so the sources do not determine which of the two is intended.

**Chronology note (inference):** The only death year the sources state directly is 景元二年 for 州泰, which is 261 CE. For 周泰 the source states only 「黃武中卒」[3], giving no year, so no date is assigned to him here.

q: What happened when Zhuge Liang used the Empty Fort Strategy at Yangping to scare off Sima Yi?
reply:
## Conclusion

The "Empty Fort" episode at Yangping (陽平) is **not in Chen Shou's main text** of the *Sanguozhi*. It survives only as a story by **Guo Chong (郭沖), quoted in Pei Songzhi's commentary to the Zhuge Liang biography** — and Pei Songzhi himself argues it never happened, because Sima Yi was nowhere near Yangping at the time.

## What the story says (Guo Chong's account)

According to Guo Chong's 《三事》:

- Zhuge Liang was camped at Yangping and had sent Wei Yan and the other armies east, leaving only 10,000 men to hold the town. Sima Yi (called 晉宣帝 in the text) came with 200,000 troops and, missing Wei Yan's column, arrived about 60 *li* away; scouts reported that Zhuge Liang's force in the town was small and weak.
- Zhuge Liang, unable to reach Wei Yan in time, stayed calm: 「敕軍中皆臥旗息鼓，不得妄出菴幔，又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒。」[1] — "he ordered the army to lower its banners and silence its drums, not to come out of their tents, and had all four gates thrown wide open and the ground swept and sprinkled."
- Because Sima Yi "had always considered Zhuge Liang cautious," and now suddenly saw this show of weakness, 「疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山」[1] — he suspected an ambush and led his army north toward the hills.
- The next day Zhuge Liang laughed and said: 「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣。」[1] — "Sima Yi must think I am afraid and that there is a strong ambush, so he has gone off along the mountains." Scouts confirmed it, and Sima Yi later "deeply regretted" it [1].

Pei Songzhi rejects the whole thing. The objection quoted in the commentary states:

The pinyin "Zhang Yi" matches **three** different Shu-Han figures in the *Sanguozhi*. I'll give each one.

## 1. Zhang Yi 张裔 (courtesy Zhang Junsi 君嗣)

A civil official and administrator, who spent years as a captive in Wu before returning to serve as Zhuge Liang's Chief Clerk of the Rear.

- He was from Chengdu, Shu commandery, studied the *Gongyang Commentary* and was widely read in the *Shiji* and *Hanshu*; under Liu Zhang he was made a xiaolian, served as magistrate of Yufu, then as a staff officer and acting Commander of the Guard: 「張裔字君嗣，蜀郡成都人也。治《公羊春秋》，博涉《史》、《漢》」[1]; 「劉璋時，舉孝廉，為魚復長，還州署從事，領帳下司馬」[1].
- He was given troops to resist Zhang Fei: 「璋授裔兵，拒張飛於德陽陌下，軍敗，還成都」[1]. He was sent as Liu Zhang's envoy to Liu Bei and arranged the peaceful opening of the city gates: 「為璋奉使詣先主，先主許以禮其君而安其人也，裔還，城門乃開」[1].
- As Administrator of Yizhou he was seized by the local leader Yong Kai: 「闓遂趑趄不賓，假鬼教曰：『張府君如瓠壺，外雖澤而內實粗，不足殺，令縛與吳。』於是遂送裔於權」[1].
- After Liu Bei's death Zhuge Liang had Deng Zhi ask for his return: 「會先主薨，諸葛亮遣鄧芝使吳，亮令芝言次可從權請裔」[3]. Sun Quan only met him at the moment of departure — 「裔臨發，權乃引見」[3] — and Zhang Yi's quick, mocking answers made Sun Quan eager to keep him, so Zhang Yi regretted not having played dumb and fled by boat: 「裔出閣，深悔不能陽愚，即便就船，倍道兼行」[3].
- Back in Shu he became Zhuge Liang's Canjun and then, with the rank of Colonel of Archers, **Liufu Zhangshi (Chief Clerk of the Rear)**: 「丞相亮以為參軍，署府事，又領益州治中從事。亮出駐漢中，裔以射聲校尉領留府長史」[2]. He said 「公賞不遺遠，罰不阿近，爵不可以無功取，刑不可以貴勢免」[2], and joked that people were honoring the office, not him: 「人自敬丞相長史，男子張君嗣附之，疲倦欲死」[2].
- He was criticized by Yang Hong as able at hard tasks but "unfair by nature": 「裔天姿明察，長於治劇，才誠堪之，然性不公平，恐不可專任」[4]. He quarreled with Cen Shu, drawing a long reproachful letter from Zhuge Liang [4].

## 2. Zhang Ni 张嶷 (courtesy Zhang Boqi 伯岐)

A military man, famous for pacifying the southwest and for dying in battle at Didao.

- From Nanchongguo, Ba commandery: 「張嶷字伯岐，巴郡南充國人也」[11]. As a young man he saved his county magistrate's wife from bandits: 「嶷冒白刃，攜負夫人，夫人得免」[11].

- Under Ma Zhong he fought the Qiang and the southern peoples [11]; 裴注引《益部耆舊傳》 gives details of his campaigns, where he was 「戰鬥常冠軍首，遂斬冑」[25].
- He was made **Administrator of Yuexi**, where the office had long been a dead letter: 「是後太守不敢之郡，只住安定縣，去郡八百餘里，其郡徒有名而已」[26]. He pacified the tribes by kindness and force, capturing and then releasing the chief Wei Lang: 「嶷乃往討，生縛其帥魏狼。又解縱告喻，使招懷餘類」[26]. He governed there fifteen years with the region at peace, and when he left, 「夷民戀慕，扶轂泣涕」[14].
- On his death: when the Wei magistrate of Didao, Li Jian, offered to surrender, 「魏狄道長李簡密書請降，衛將軍姜維率嶷等因簡之資以出隴西」[14]; 裴注引《益部耆舊傳》 says the court was doubtful but Zhang Ni insisted it was genuine, and though crippled by rheumatism he begged to go, telling the Later Ruler he would repay the favor with his life: 「李簡請降，眾議狐疑，而嶷曰必然」[16]; 「若涼州克定，臣為籓表守將；若有未捷，殺身以報」[16].

## 3. Zhang Yi 张翼 (courtesy Zhang Bogong 伯恭)

A general and administrator, known as the man who stood up to Jiang Wei.

- From Wuyang, Jianwei; his great-grandfather was the Situ Zhang Hao and his great-grandfather the Guangling Administrator Zhang Gang: 「張翼字伯恭，犍為武陽人也。高祖父司空浩，曾祖父廣陵太守綱，皆有名跡」[9].
- He served as Administrator of several commanderies, then as **Qubing Duhu**; when recalled during the Liu Zhou rebellion he refused to leave before his replacement arrived: 「代人未至，吾方臨戰場，當運糧積穀，為滅賊之資，豈可以黜退之故而廢公家之務乎？」[9].
- He is most famous for opposing Jiang Wei's repeated campaigns: 「唯翼廷爭，以為國小民勞，不宜黷武」[21]. After Jiang Wei's great victory over Wang Jing, Zhang Yi advised stopping and Jiang Wei angrily accused him of 「為蛇畫足」[21]. From then on Jiang Wei disliked him but kept dragging him along: 「自翼建異論，維心與翼不善，然常牽率同行，翼亦不得已而往」[21]. The official verdict is 「張翼亢姜維之銳」[22].
- At the fall of Shu he was at Jiange with Jiang Wei and surrendered with him to Zhong Hui at Fu: 「與維咸在劍閣，共詣降鍾會於涪」[21]. In 景耀六年 = **263 CE** he went to Chengdu with Zhong Hui in the following first month and was killed by mutinous soldiers: 「明年正月，隨會至成都，為亂兵所殺」[21].

**In short:** if the question is about administration and the Shu court, it is Zhang Yi 张裔; if about the southern frontier and a soldier's death in battle, Zhang Ni 张嶷; if about opposing Jiang Wei and the fall of Shu, Zhang Yi 张翼.

## 2. Zhang Ni 张嶷 (courtesy Zhang Boqi 伯岐)

A military man, famous for pacifying the southwest and for dying in battle at Didao.

- From Nanchongguo, Ba commandery: 「張嶷字伯岐，巴郡南充國人也」[11]. As a young man he saved his county magistrate's wife from bandits: 「嶷冒白刃，攜負夫人，夫人得免」[11].
- He lured the bandit Zhang Mu and his men to a banquet and killed them: 「乃詐與和親，剋期置酒」[11]; 「因斬慕等五十餘級」[11].
- Under Ma Zhong he fought the Qiang and the southern peoples [11]; 裴注引《益部耆舊傳》 gives details of his campaigns, where he was 「戰鬥常冠軍首，遂斬冑」[25].
- He was made **Administrator of Yuexi**, where the office had long been a dead letter: 「是後太守不敢之郡，只住安定縣，去郡八百餘里，其郡徒有名而已」[26]. He pacified the tribes by kindness and force, capturing and then releasing the chief Wei Lang: 「嶷乃往討，生縛其帥魏狼。又解縱告喻，使招懷餘類」[26]. - On his death: when the Wei magistrate of Didao, Li Jian, offered to surrender, 「魏狄道長李簡密書請降，衛將軍姜維率嶷等因簡之資以出隴西」[14]; 裴注引《益部耆舊傳》 says the court was doubtful but Zhang Ni insisted it was genuine, and though crippled by rheumatism he begged to go, telling the Later Ruler he would repay the favor with his life: 「李簡請降，眾議狐疑，而嶷曰必然」[16]; 「若涼州克定，臣為籓表守將；若有未捷，殺身以報」[16].
- At Didao the army met the Wei general Xu Zhi: 「嶷臨陣隕身，然其所殺傷亦過倍」[14]. The year given is 延熙十七年 = **254 CE** [14]. The southern peoples wept and built shrines to him: 「南土越崔巂民夷聞嶷死，無不悲泣，為嶷立廟，四時水旱輒祀之」[14].
- 裴注引《益部耆舊傳》 praises him: 「而其策略足以入算，果烈足以立威」, and says 「後主深崇之」[12]. The *Sanguozhi* verdict calls him 「識斷明果」[15].

## 3. Zhang Yi 张翼 (courtesy Zhang Bogong 伯恭)

A general and administrator, known as the man who stood up to Jiang Wei.

- From Wuyang, Jianwei; his great-grandfather was the Situ Zhang Hao and his great-grandfather the Guangling Administrator Zhang Gang: 「張翼字伯恭，犍為武陽人也。高祖父司空浩，曾祖父廣陵太守綱，皆有名跡」[9].
- He served as Administrator of several commanderies, then as **Qubing Duhu**; when recalled during the Liu Zhou rebellion he refused to leave before his replacement arrived: 「代人未至，吾方臨戰場，當運糧積穀，為滅賊之資，豈可以黜退之故而廢公家之務乎？」[9].
- He is most famous for opposing Jiang Wei's repeated campaigns: 「唯翼廷爭，以為國小民勞，不宜黷武」[21]. After Jiang Wei's great victory over Wang Jing, Zhang Yi advised stopping and Jiang Wei angrily accused him of 「為蛇畫足」[21]. From then on Jiang Wei disliked him but kept dragging him along: 「自翼建異論，維心與翼不善，然常牽率同行，翼亦不得已而往」[21]. The official verdict is 「張翼亢姜維之銳」[22].
- At the fall of Shu he was at Jiange with Jiang Wei and surrendered with him to Zhong Hui at Fu: 「與維咸在劍閣，共詣降鍾會於涪」[21]. In 景耀六年 = **263 CE** he went to Chengdu with Zhong Hui in the following first month and was killed by mutinous soldiers: 「明年正月，隨會至成都，為亂兵所殺」[21].

**In short:** if the question is about administration and the Shu court, it is Zhang Yi 张裔; if about the southern frontier and a soldier's death in battle, Zhang Ni 张嶷; if about opposing Jiang Wei and the fall of Shu, Zhang Yi 张翼.

q: Tell me about Liu Yan.
reply:
The name "Liu Yan" corresponds to three different men in the *Sanguozhi*: 劉焉 (Liu Yan, courtesy name Junlang), 劉琰 (Liu Yan, courtesy name Weishuo), and 劉延 (Liu Yan, a general with no biography). The most famous is the first, so I'll focus on him and then briefly note the others.

## 劉焉 Liu Yan (字 君郎), Governor of Yi Province

**Origins and early career.** He was a native of Jingling in Jiangxia and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han imperial house: 「劉焉字君郎，江夏竟陵人也，漢魯恭王之後裔」[1]. He served in the provinces and, as a member of the imperial clan, was made a Palace Gentleman (中郎); after his teacher Zhu Gong died he left office, lived on Yangcheng Mountain teaching, and went on to hold a series of posts including Prefect of Luoyang, Inspector of Ji Province, Administrator of Nanyang, and the court offices of 宗正 and 太常 [1].

**The proposal that made him a "shepherd."** Seeing Emperor Ling's government in decline, he proposed that the court appoint men of clean reputation as *mubo* (牧伯, provincial shepherds) to pacify the realm: 「可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏」[1]. He himself first wanted the post of Governor of Jiaozhi to escape the coming troubles, but the Palace Attendant Dong Fu privately told him, "The capital will fall into chaos; the field of Yi Province has the aura of a Son of Heaven," and so he turned his mind to Yi: 「京師將亂，益州分野有天子氣」[1].

**Appointment as Governor of Yi.** When the Inspector of Yi, Xi Jian, extorted from the people and the provinces of Bing and Liang killed their own inspectors, Liu Yan's plan was carried out. He was sent out as Army-Inspecting Envoy and acting Governor of Yi, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yangcheng, with orders to arrest Xi Jian: 「出為監軍使者，領益州牧，封陽城侯，當收儉治罪」[5]. Dong Fu and Zhao Wei went with him [5]. The *Xu Han Shu* (裴注引《續漢書》) records that at this time Liu Yu was given You, Liu Yan Yi, Liu Biao Jing, and Jia Cong Ji [3]. The *Han Lingdi Ji* (裴注引《漢靈帝紀》) says the emperor received Liu Yan and appointed him Inspector of Yi, and that because the roads were blocked he halted at the eastern border of Jing [3]. (Note: 裴松之按 points out that Liu Biao became Inspector of Jing only after Sun Jian killed Wang Rui, so he was not contemporaneous with Liu Yan in that post [3].)

**Taking control of Yi.** When Ma Xiang and Zhao Zhi raised the Yellow Turban banner at Mianzhu and killed Xi Jian, the provincial official Jia Long defeated them and welcomed Liu Yan. Liu Yan moved his seat to Mianzhu, treated the people generously, and secretly plotted: 「焉徙治綿竹，撫納離叛，務行寬惠，陰圖異計」[10]. He sent Zhang Lu as Commander of Supervisory Righteousness to stay in Hanzhong, cut the roads, and kill the court's envoys, then reported that "rice-bandits" had blocked the way. He also killed over ten local strongmen, including Wang Xian and Li Quan, to establish his authority, and struck down the Administrator of Jianwei, Ren Qi, and Jia Long when they turned against him [10]. The *Yingxiong Ji* (裴注引《英雄記》) says Liu Yan raised troops but did not join the realm in punishing Dong Zhuo, keeping to his province to defend himself [7].

**Ambitions and family tragedy.** His ambitions grew; he had more than a thousand carriages and equipages made for imperial use, and Liu Biao memorialized that this resembled Zixia at Xihe: 「焉意漸盛，造作乘輿車具千馀乘」[31]. His sons Liu Fan, Liu Dan, and Liu Zhang were all at Chang'an with Emperor Xian, while only Liu Mao was with him [31]. The emperor sent Liu Zhang to reason with him, but Liu Yan kept Liu Zhang and would not send him back [31]; the *Dianlue* (裴注引《典略》) says he feigned illness to summon Liu Zhang [32]. When Ma Teng rose at Mei, Liu Yan and Liu Fan conspired with him to attack Chang'an. The plot leaked, Ma Teng was defeated, and Liu Fan was killed and Liu Dan executed; the *Yingxiong Ji* adds that Liu Fan fled to Ma Teng's camp to beg for troops and that Liu Yan sent Colonel Sun Zhao, who was defeated at Chang'an [31][33].

**Death and succession.** Fire from heaven burned his city, destroying his carriages and spreading to the people's homes. He moved his seat to Chengdu, and grieving for his sons and shaken by the calamity, he died of a carbuncle on his back in the first year of Xingping (194 CE): 「興平元年，癰疽發背而卒」[6]. Zhao Wei and other great officials, favoring Liu Zhang's mildness, put him forward as Inspector of Yi, and the court confirmed him as Army-Inspecting Envoy and acting Governor of Yi [6].

## The other two men named Liu Yan

- **劉琰 (字 威碩)**, a native of Lu, was recruited by the First Sovereign (Liu Bei) in Yu Province. After Liu Bei settled Yi, he made him Administrator of Guling; under the Later Sovereign he became Commandant of the Guards, Army-Instructor, General of the Rear, and then General of Chariots and Cavalry, though he took no part in state affairs and merely kept about a thousand troops [11]. He was notoriously extravagant, keeping dozens of singing maidservants [11]. In the tenth year of Jianxing he quarreled with Wei Yan and was rebuked by Zhuge Liang; he wrote a letter of apology [11]. In the first month of the twelfth year, his wife Lady Hu, after a month-long stay in the palace, was beaten and divorced by him on suspicion; she reported him, and he was executed in the marketplace: 「琰竟棄市」[13].
- **劉延**, a general with no separate biography. He appears as the Administrator of Dong Province whom Yuan Shao's generals Guo Tu, Chunyu Qiong, and Yan Liang attacked at Baima, prompting Cao Cao to come north to his rescue [21][22]. This is the 劉延 listed in the records, distinct from the two above.

**Following is not from the *Sanguozhi*:** There is nothing here that contradicts the *Sanguozhi*, so no novel-based note is needed. (The three men are simply homophones in modern pinyin and must be told apart by context.)

After Liu Bei settled Yi, he made him Administrator of Guling; under the Later Sovereign he became Commandant of the Guards, Army-Instructor, General of the Rear, and then General of Chariots and Cavalry, though he took no part in state affairs and merely kept about a thousand troops [11]. He was notoriously extravagant, keeping dozens of singing maidservants [11]. In the tenth year of Jianxing he quarreled with Wei Yan and was rebuked by Zhuge Liang; he wrote a letter of apology [11]. In the first month of the twelfth year, his wife Lady Hu, after a month-long stay in the palace, was beaten and divorced by him on suspicion; she reported him, and he was executed in the marketplace: 「琰竟棄市」[13].
- **劉延**, a general with no separate biography. He appears as the Administrator of Dong Province whom Yuan Shao's generals Guo Tu, Chunyu Qiong, and Yan Liang attacked at Baima, prompting Cao Cao to come north to his rescue [21][22]. This is the 劉延 listed in the records, distinct from the two above.

**Following is not from the *Sanguozhi*:** There is nothing here that contradicts the *Sanguozhi*, so no novel-based note is needed. (The three men are simply homophones in modern pinyin and must be told apart by context.)

## 劉焉 Liu Yan (字 君郎), Governor of Yi Province

**Origins and early career.** He was a native of Jingling in Jiangxia and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han imperial house: 「劉焉字君郎，江夏竟陵人也，漢魯恭王之後裔」[1]. He served in the provinces and, as a member of the imperial clan, was made a Palace Gentleman (中郎); after his teacher Zhu Gong died he left office, lived on Yangcheng Mountain teaching, was recommended as "filial and incorrupt," and summoned to the office of the Minister over the Masses, going on to hold a series of posts including Prefect of Luoyang, Inspector of Ji Province, Administrator of Nanyang, and the court offices of 宗正 and 太常 [1]. Pei Songzhi notes that Zhu Gong was the Minister over the Masses Zhu Tian: 「臣松之案：祝公，司徒祝恬也」[34].

**The proposal that made him a "shepherd."** Seeing Emperor Ling's government in decline, he proposed that the court appoint men of clean reputation as *mubo* (牧伯, provincial shepherds) to pacify the realm: 「可選清名重臣以為牧伯，鎮安方夏」[1]. He himself first wanted the post of Governor of Jiaozhi to escape the coming troubles: 「焉內求交阯牧，欲避世難」[1]. But the Palace Attendant Dong Fu of Guanghan privately told him, "The capital will fall into chaos; the field of Yi Province has the aura of a Son of Heaven," and so he turned his mind to Yi: 「京師將亂，益州分野有天子氣」[1].

**Appointment as Governor of Yi.** When the Inspector of Yi, Xi Jian, extorted from the people, and the provinces of Bing and Liang killed their own inspectors, Liu Yan's plan was carried out [5].
